transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-02
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (Sunbridge ML), Priya Iyer (Sunbridge Platform), Evan Brooks (Sunbridge PM)

Summary:
Quick scoping call to align on workload temporal-skew (burstiness), QPS/concurrency targets, token input/output distribution, and POC benchmark plan + timeline. Key ask: reproduce realistic bursts (short, high-QPS spikes), measure p95/p99 under mixed token lengths, validate caching/batching strategies and provide cost estimates.

Topics covered:
- Workload shape & temporal skew (daily + promotional bursts)
- Concurrency vs QPS mapping and cold-start effects
- Input/output token histograms and tail cases
- Benchmark types: replay, poisson ramp, burst-fingerprinting test
- Success criteria (latency SLOs, error budget, cost targets)
- Timeline & infra access (VPC peering + credentials)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex: Alright everyone, thanks for joining, uh, this is Alex from Redwood. Quick intros, then we'll jump into the traffic and token shape.
[00:15] Jordan: Jordan here, ML eng, I'll own the model integration side and provide the traffic traces. Priya on infra will handle peering.
[00:22] Priya: Yep, hi, Priya. we'll handle networking.
[00:28] Alex: Great. Maya, you want to kick off with what we typically look for in a temporal skew POC?
[00:34] Maya: Sure, real quick. For these retail workloads we usually see low baseline QPS with sharp promotional bursts. The point is not just peak QPS but the burst duration and inter-arrival patterns — whether it's a 3–5 minute flash or a sustained hour-long spike changes everything.
[00:48] Evan: To add context, our Black Friday-like loads are unpredictable. Last year a promo caused a 20x spike for about six minutes then decayed; the cold-start latencies hurt us.
[00:58] Jordan: And token lengths vary: most queries are 10–80 input tokens, but some generative responses go 800–2500 tokens (order confirmations with history). So tail tokens are important.
[01:12] Maya: That's a big signal — we need the 95th/99th token length percentiles. Also KV cache reuse for chat/historic context will reduce throughput but changes latencies.
[01:26] Alex: Can you give us ballpark QPS numbers you care about? Baseline and burst?
[01:30] Priya: Baseline is about 4–6 QPS worldwide. Peak bursts we've seen up to ~240 QPS for short windows. Our target is to survive bursts with less than 1% error and p95 latency under 1 second on typical prompts.
[01:44] Maya: Note that p95 for long-output responses will naturally be higher; we usually split SLOs by token tier — short (<128 out) p95 < 500–600ms, medium (128–512) < 900ms, long >512 we accept higher but want to quantify.
[01:58] Jordan: Also, concurrency — during bursts we hit 70–140 concurrent requests depending on model and batching.
[02:07] Alex: Useful. For the POC we'll want: 1) replay of real traces, 2) synthetic burst-fingerprinting (short intense spikes), 3) ramp tests to measure steady-state throughput and queuing. We'll measure p50/p95/p99, token/sec, GPU utilization, and cost per 1M tokens.
[02:26] Evan: How do you handle batching + latency tradeoff? If we set aggressive batching to improve throughput, tail latencies grow.
[02:34] Maya: Right — Redwood runtime supports continuous batching with per-model policies. For POC we'll test a few profiles: low-latency (batch size <=4, prefer immediate dispatch), balanced, and throughput (larger batches). We'll run scenarios under each to report the econ/latency tradeoff.
[02:50] Jordan: Do you support prefix/KV caching? We have many repeated context prefixes.
[02:55] Alex: Yes, KV/prefix caching is supported. We'll measure cache hit rates and the effective tokens saved. Keep in mind caching changes burst load — if cache warms, GPU work per call drops.
[03:06] Priya: Security & compliance — we need SOC2 & VPC/PEERING details, and KMS for keys.
[03:12] Alex: We'll share the security pack and SOC2 artifact. For the private POC we'll use VPC peering and customer-managed KMS; that's standard.
[03:20] Evan: For the benchmark, what's the recommended test harness? We prefer replay vs synthetic.
[03:25] Maya: Replay is best for fidelity but we also augment with poisson and heavy-tailed arrival models to stress tails. We'll provide a client container (curl/java/python) that can replay logs and optionally vary token sizes.
[03:37] Jordan: We can anonymize and drop PII from traces. Expect a 14-day log.
[03:41] Alex: Perfect. On metrics: we'll capture request-level tensors: request_id, arrival_ts, start_exec, end_exec, tokens_in, tokens_out, error_code, model_variant, kernel/quantization used. Also measure warm vs cold path (first request to a model variant after scale-up).
[03:59] Priya: Cold path measuring is important; we saw 1.8s extra on cold starts last time. Can you simulate scale-up events?
[04:06] Maya: Yes, we'll do step-ramp tests where we force node additions and capture the scaling tail. We'll also test graceful fallback to smaller variants if the preferred model is oversubscribed.
[04:18] Evan: Bench timeline? How long till we have initial results?
[04:22] Alex: Proposed timeline: Week 0 (this week) - access & trace handoff; Week 1 - Redwood sets up bench infra, containerize client; Week 2 - run replay + ramp tests; Week 3 - analyze and iterate on tuning (batching/cache/quant), Week 4 - handoff & review + go/no-go. So roughly 3–4 weeks for initial POC.
[04:44] Jordan: That seems fast but doable. We need a business-level success criteria doc.
[04:49] Alex: Agreed — draft proposal: (1) Functional: serve 95% of production mix with p95 < 750ms (short/med tiers weighted), error rate < 1%. (2) Economics: cost per 1M tokens <= target (we'll compute based on profile), and (3) Operational: VPC peering + audit logs present. Final sign-off by Evan.
[05:08] Evan: Fine. Also include regression tests for hallucination on longer generations — not just perf.
[05:13] Maya: We'll include token-level quality checks — run sample prompts pre/post-quantization and measure semantic similarity.
[05:20] Jordan: About the model variants — we may want quantized variants for cost saving, but worried about quality.
[05:25] Alex: We'll validate three variants: FP16 baseline, 4-bit quantized, and a distill/cheaper variant. We'll include eval prompts and a small human review subset.
[05:36] Priya: Networking — what's the bandwidth requirement per GPU? We need to size egress.
[05:40] Maya: For typical generative workloads bandwidth is moderate; token streaming increases egress. We'll provide expected peak Mbps per concurrent long-output request; approximate numbers in the runbook.
[05:50] Jordan: Can you also expose internal traces (stack traces/timings)? Our infra team will want them for correlation.
[05:54] Alex: Yes we'll include tracing hooks and a mapping to their observability. We'll redact secrets.
[06:01] Evan: Any competing solutions we should consider? We evaluated Anthropic and a Vertex-hosted approach, but they lacked predictable burst economics.
[06:10] Alex: Noted. For the POC we'll include competitor-fair tests if you want.
[06:14] Jordan: Ok. small practical Qs: what do you need from us right now?
[06:18] Alex: Primary ask: upload anonymized 14-day traffic logs + sample of the heaviest 1% of requests (by token). Also provide an initial SLO matrix: latency by token tier and error budget.
[06:28] Jordan: I'll own that, expect upload by Monday.
[06:31] Priya: We'll provision VPC peering and a read-only service account.
[06:34] Maya: We'll push the client image to the registry and post instructions. Link will be in the runbook (we'll share internally).
[06:41] Alex: I'll also send the benchmark spreadsheet with tabs for QPS scenarios, token histograms, cost calcs, and the proposed success criteria.
[06:48] Evan: Let's capture acceptance criteria again: 95% of production-mix requests p95 < 750ms, errors <1%, and cost per 1M tokens below your computed threshold. If we hit these, we'll discuss Dedicated reserved capacity.
[07:05] Maya: We'll also provide the traces for cold-start behavior and node-add events.
[07:12] Jordan: One more thing, our data residency: logs must remain in EU region for EU traffic — can we pin region for those traces?
[07:20] Alex: Yes, we can run region-scoped clusters and will respect residency. We'll note that in the runbook.
[07:27] Evan: Great. Any blockers?
[07:29] Priya: None that can't be resolved quick. Just need the service account and a test window.
[07:34] Alex: Cool. We'll schedule the 3-hour window for 12/08 UTC and share the runbook + container links by 12/04.
[07:41] Jordan: Sounds good. thanks.
[07:44] Alex: Thanks everyone — recap and email follow-up with artifacts.
